最近看您的帖子又多了一层思考，因为刚去了一趟丽江、大理，对于中西方建筑文化上的差异有了一些新的体会。首先，我感觉人文思想的差异决定了建筑文化上的差异。欧洲人似乎有与生俱来的创造力，而且他们崇尚个性，于是造就了色彩丰富、千姿百态的小镇街道。而中国人崇尚礼仪，反对张扬个性，于是中国的古镇在建筑色彩和形式上都更趋同一些。另一方面，中国文化自古以来视建筑等同于舆服车马，不求永存。从来不把建筑作为一种学术。古代文人更是崇尚俭朴，把“大兴土木”一贯列为劳民伤财的事。对于崇伟新巧的建筑贬多于褒。技术由师徒相传，以实地操作、心传口授为主。读书人很少有人关心建筑，术书也很少。所以，即使如楼上那位所希望的将长安城完整保留下来，恐怕也难看到如欧洲小镇般的丰富多彩，因为都城均比附于《周礼考工记》的王城之制，大多外形方正、街道平直、按一定规划建造。

Mainz was proclaimed the Holy See during Willigis' reign (975-1011). This archbishop, simultaneously Arch chancellor of the First German Empire, started to build it for the Ottons in 975, modelling it on the old St Peter's cathedral in Rome. Seven coronations took place in the Mainz cathedral. The new cathedral did not, however, survive the day of its consecration in August 1009 - a fire destroyed the building and the cathedral could only be used again in 1036. Willigis was therefore not buried in the cathedral, but in St. Stephen's. The bronze door leaves of the market portals, the oldest pieces of equipment in the Roman pillar basilica, nevertheless originated during his rule, in the 10th century. The inscriptions on this ceremonial door list its constructors and artists. The cathedral has three naves, a double chancel, and numerous chapels. The west chancel with the main altar is dedicated to St Martin, and the east chancel to St Stephen.

The buildings surrounding the Mainz cathedral are still intact, retaining the same form as when they were constructed. The red tinted sand-stone mountain of a cathedral which grew over the centuries, has a foothill in the light coloured stone of the Roman Gotthard Chapel, that archbishop Adalbert erected before 1137 as a private chapel. A crucifix from the period of the Hohenstaufen Emperors is preserved in this chapel.

In 1778/79 Ignaz Michael Neumann, the son of the famous baroque architect Balthasar Neumann, built the cathedral houses on the burial grounds. As there was a great fear of fire due to the cathedral having been set alight seven times over the centuries, these cathedral buildings were constructed with fire proof stone roofs. After being hit by lightning, the west tower was given a new steeple top in the form of a reproduction of the past architectural styles in 1767. This was, however, built in stone, and not as previously in wood.
The east chancel, with walls measuring over two metres in thickness, is the oldest part of the cathedral. The east tower was partly destroyed in the 1793 bombardment of Mainz by the empire's troops. It was rebuilt as a chancel tower in the 19th century. The city architect Georg Moller designed its round iron dome, which was later removed to be replaced by a more historic pointed roof. The beautiful external adornments (approx. 1100) were sculpted by stone masons from Lombardy. In the 19th century an 11th century crypt was found under the east chancel. In the l5th century a Gothic belfry was added to the late Roman west chancel (which was built between 1200 and 1239). The sale of the carved rococo choir stalls of 1767 was prevented by Bishop Joseph Ludwig Colmar, who was appointed by Napoleon. It was also Colmar who convinced the French Emperor not to demolish the cathedral after the secularisation of 1803. Ever since 1928 bishops have been buried under the west chancel. Of the 84 post-Bonifatius bishops, 45 are buried in the cathedral. A large number of tomb stones and memorials from the 11th to the 20th centuries adorn the walls and pillars of this church and cloister. Whoever briefly examines these memorials to dignitaries of the past wanders through history.
These sculptures are the greatest treasure bequeathed, as old wall and glass paintings are not to be found in the cathedral. The wall paintings in the middle nave by the Nazarene Philipp Veit date back to the last century. The Lady altar in the Ketteler Chapel, with it's "beautiful Mainzerin" is a centre of attraction. The late Gothic wooden sculpture (approx. 1510) is in the series of the wooden carvings by Hans Backoffens, to whom one can also accredit three grave memorials. The 15th century cloister has, two storeys. In the past the canons lived in the chapter. Today the Episcopal and Diocesan Museum is housed there, in which sacred treasures from many eras are preserved and displayed.

The quarter surrounding the cathedral and the system of alleys to the South, called "Vilzbach" locally, is the part of town where local traditions have stayed alive. Carl Zuckmayer's term "Kelter Europas" fits this area best; after two decades of extensive reconstruction the area of Leichhof, Leichhofstraße, Augustinerstraße, Kirschgarten and Hollagässchen now show a comfortable romantic ambience, reminiscent of the South, especially when there is a market day with flowers and culinary delicacies abounding on the Markt, on Höfchen and Liebfrauenplatz. The six spires of the thousand-year old Dom dominate the scenery. The fapades of the residences on the Markt, and the fountain from 1526, the finest example of early renaissance fountains in Germany, are further attractive points.

Visitors are also attracted by St Stephen's Church on the hill with the same name. In 1985, the late Marc Chagall created a unique cycle of stained-glass windows with scenes from the Old Testament. The dominant blue give a mystic light to the entire choir part of the church.

The impact on the world by Mainz’s native son John Gooseflesh, better known as Johannes Gutenberg, the inventor of movable type printing is of such consequence that he is considered to be the most important individual-contributor of the the Second Millennium. Within 25 years of the introduction of type, ideas and ideologies were spread that rent the very fabric of Western civilization and the Christian world. Simultaneously the Ages of Discovery and of Mercantilism and Colonization evolved as discoveries and travel were publicized in printed reports and books. The long, arduous, costly process of hand-written works and copies carried out by scribes and monks on tablets, parchment and rudimentary paper, a process some 4,000 years old or more abruptly ended. The printed word using re-useable cold-type setting allowed everyone access to knowledge and spelled an eventual end to Feudalism, absolute control of lives by Church and State, the spread of orthodox and revolutionary thoughts and ideas, and of life itself. Literacy evolved and liberty followed. All lives on Earth were changed forever by the printing press

Based on Gutenberg’s invention, hot-type printing and now electronic information transferral came about. The Information Age is now, the World Wide Web, internet, computers all descendents and variations of Gutenberg’s pioneering work.

其实翻译成罗马风还是很有道理的，因为：1. 的确当初是从古罗马的建筑中吸取了一些成分，甚至当时的人自己都自诩罗马风；2. 文艺复兴的时候有些人根本就把一些罗曼时代的建筑误当成古罗马的，比如佛罗伦萨的圣乔万尼礼拜堂和山顶的San Miniato教堂；3. 西方文字中的romanesque和romanik意思确实是“罗马的风格”。但是翻译到中文来，仅仅靠加一个“风”字以区别相隔700年的建筑，实在太容易造成误解，所以我自己从来都用罗曼。

关于阿尔俾斯以北文艺复兴的说法，我也不大敢苟同。似乎有点附庸风雅的感觉。就象Bamberg还有一处沿河风景，自谕为“小威尼斯”。由此也想到国内某些地方，自谕为“东方XXX", 大概人总是喜欢借一些知名的东西装点一下自己。
其实我不是说它们不好，它们也的确就是德国的文艺复兴时代的风格了。我也不知道该怎么说，就是觉得比较好玩，从意大利文艺复兴学了写皮毛并和旧风格混起来，与文艺复兴的主旨反而倒背离了。但从另一方面，它们融入了地方特色，也是好事，否则世界被千篇一律的东西扫荡更不好。从这个角度，我倒也喜欢有些东西俗气一点、不伦不类一点。
